entry.name: Declarative Question
entry.pattern: Question[closed, same-polarity bias] applied to Declarative Clause + question intonation

dimensions.form: Declarative Clause syntax, without subject–auxiliary inversion, combined with question intonation or corresponding question punctuation
dimensions.meaning: A polar question strongly biased toward the answer with the same propositional content and polarity as the declarative base
dimensions.function: Typically seeks confirmation of a proposition the speaker is already inclined to accept
dimensions.distribution: Independent declarative Clauses in confirmation-seeking and other strongly biased question contexts

1.definition: A declarative Clause used as a strongly same-polarity-biased question through question prosody
1.details: Positive declarative questions are biased toward a positive answer and negative declarative questions toward a negative answer. The expected answer therefore has the same propositional content as the question, and confirmatory responses such as That's right, Exactly, and Quite so are especially natural. Question is the semantic category applied to a syntactically declarative Clause, with question intonation marking the combination; the host does not change clause type. It is not an echo question, since it need not repeat or query the wording of a prior stimulus (CGEL pp. 879–83).

examples.note: Positive declarative question biased toward confirmation that they have finished
Negative declarative question biased toward confirmation that they have not finished

examples.form: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
examples.note: Confidence marker reinforces the positive bias while remaining outside question scope

examples.form: [There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]
examples.note: Natural confirmation-seeking declarative question with negative polarity

constraints.description: The Clause retains declarative syntax and is headed by VP; there is no clause-type-triggered subject–auxiliary inversion.
Question intonation in speech, or corresponding question punctuation in writing, supplies the question interpretation without changing declarative clause type.
Question is a semantic classification of the whole form–interpretation pairing, while declarative remains the syntactic type of the headed host Clause.
The construction is strongly epistemically biased toward the same-polarity answer and is infelicitous as a neutral request between equally open positive and negative alternatives.
No prior utterance is required. If the form instead queries whether particular wording was said or heard, the independent echo-question construction is involved.

projection.target: Declarative order plus question prosody predicts strong same-polarity bias, confirmation-seeking function, and compatibility with responses such as That's right or Exactly, in contrast to a neutral closed interrogative
projection.evidence: Positive and negative declarative questions consistently reverse neither polarity nor expected answer; their response profile and confidence-marker compatibility diagnose bias independently of declarative word order

grounds.note: Question interpretation applied to declarative form projects polarity bias and response profile
The same-polarity bias recurs across positive and negative declarative questions

known_boundary_items: She is a genius?: ordinary declarative question if it asks whether she is a genius; echo question if it asks whether the speaker said that she is

relatedConstructions.notes: Declarative Question is the same-polarity-biased subtype realized on a declarative Clause
The syntactic host retains declarative Clause type while receiving question semantics
Closed interrogatives use interrogative syntax and can be neutral; declarative questions retain declarative syntax and are strongly biased
Echo questions depend on a stimulus and question some aspect of that prior wording; ordinary declarative questions need not

grounds.note: Declarative questions as strongly biased indirect questions with same-polarity expectations and distinctive response patterns

curious.title: Asking by tone of voice
curious.summary: A statement-shaped sentence said with a questioning tone can ask for confirmation of something the speaker already expects.
curious.body:
They've finished? has the word order of a statement. In speech, the questioning tone turns it into a question. The speaker expects the answer yes, and a reply like That's right fits naturally.

The expectation matches the sentence. A positive one, They've finished?, expects a positive answer, and a negative one, They haven't finished?, expects a negative answer. This isn't the neutral question of Have they finished?, which leaves the answer more open. In writing, the question mark does the work of the tone.

examples.text: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
[There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]

curious.try: Say You're coming tonight? as a question. What answer do you expect? Now say Are you coming tonight? Does the expectation change?

teacher.summary: Helps explain statement-order questions that expect confirmation, as in They've finished?
teacher.explain: A declarative question keeps declarative syntax, with no subject-auxiliary inversion, and gets its question interpretation from question intonation, or question punctuation in writing. It's a closed question strongly biased toward the answer with the same propositional content and polarity as the declarative: positive toward positive, negative toward negative. Confirmatory responses such as That's right, Exactly and Quite so are especially natural. The host clause stays declarative, and question is a semantic category applied to the whole form. It is not an echo question, since it needn't repeat or query the wording of a prior utterance. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: Traditional grammars may call these statement questions or rising-intonation questions. Closed interrogative is the inverted form (Have they finished?), which can be neutral.

examples.text: [And the manager has been informed, of course?]
[There isn't any chance of her changing her mind, I take it?]

contrasts.note: Declarative syntax; biased toward a positive answer.
Closed interrogative with inversion; can be neutral.

watch_for: A learner might treat They've finished? as a neutral question, when it is biased toward a positive answer.
A learner might take They haven't finished? to expect yes, when it expects the negative answer, that they haven't.
A learner might think a declarative question must echo something just said, when no prior utterance is required.
teacher.activity: Students role-play checking a fact they half-know (a friend's plans, a test date). They ask once with an inverted question and once with a declarative question, then say how much each one assumes the answer.

child.hook: How can you ask a question without changing any words?
child.explain: You can say a sentence in a questioning voice. They've finished? You think they have, and you want to check. The other person can answer, "That's right."
child.play: Say "You're hungry" two ways, as a plain statement and then as a question. Ask a friend to listen. Can they hear which one you want an answer to?
